root.meaning: a self-governing town of the Roman state

history: Municipio goes back to the Roman state. A municipium was a town that joined Rome and accepted its duties, Latin munera, together with its rights. The word is built from munus, ‘duty, service’, and capere, ‘to take’: the citizens took on the duties. Italy has had self-governing towns for over two thousand years, and the idea never fully went away. Today municipio means the town hall, or in a large city one of its districts: Roma has fifteen municipi. In everyday speech and on official papers you will more often meet comune, the normal word for the local administration. Municipio is the building and the district, comune is the authority. English municipal is from the same Latin word.
historyEinfach: In Rome, a municipium was a town with its own government. The citizens took on duties (Latin munus) for the state. In Italian, municipio means ‘town hall’. In big cities it also means a district. For the local authority people say il Comune. English municipal comes from the same word.
